section.title: The Collection and Final Greetings
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes not with abstraction but with the concrete life of the church: a systematic collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem, Paul's travel plans and those of his coworkers, a bracing charge to be watchful and strong and to do everything in love, and warm final greetings. The resurrection hope of chapter fifteen now issues in generous giving, faithful labor, mutual love, and longing for the Lord's return, sealed with Maranatha, Come O Lord, and the grace of the Lord Jesus.
section.thesis: Gospel truth works itself out in ordinary faithfulness: giving systematically and cheerfully for the needy, laboring and traveling for the churches, standing firm and strong while doing everything in love, honoring fellow workers, and longing for the Lord's coming, so that the letter ends in grace, love, and the cry Maranatha, Come O Lord.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the collection for the saints; Paul's travel plans and his coworkers; the closing charge to be watchful, firm, strong, and loving; and the final greetings, the curse and the cry Maranatha, and the grace of Christ.

units.label: The collection for the saints
units.note: give systematically on the first day

verses.text: Now about the {{logeia|collection}} for the saints, you are to do as I directed the churches of Galatia:
On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed.
Then, on my arrival, I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem.
And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me.

units.label: Travel plans and coworkers
units.note: an open door, and faithful helpers

verses.text: After I go through Macedonia, however, I will come to you; for I will be going through Macedonia.
Perhaps I will stay with you awhile, or even spend the winter, so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go.
For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.
But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,
because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me.
If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am.
No one, then, should treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers.
Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers. He was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity.

units.label: Be watchful, firm, strong, and loving

verses.text: Be on the {{gregoreo|alert}}. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong.
Do everything in {{agape|love}}.
You know that Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Now I urge you, brothers,
to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.
I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you.
For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well. Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men.

units.label: Final greetings and Maranatha
units.note: Come, O Lord, and grace in Christ

verses.text: The churches in the province of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, and so does the church that meets at their house.
All the brothers here send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
This greeting is in my own hand, Paul.
If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!
The {{charis|grace}} of the Lord Jesus be with you.
My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

logeia.gloss: A collection, a gathering of money. Paul uses the word for the relief fund he was organizing among the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. It was not a spontaneous appeal but a planned, regular, church-wide act of love that bound the young churches to the mother church in shared grace.

gregoreo.gloss: To be awake, to stay alert, to keep watch. The first of four sharp commands that close the body of the letter. It calls the church to spiritual wakefulness against error and temptation, a watchfulness that fits a people awaiting the Lord's return.

agape.gloss: Love, the self-giving love supremely displayed in Christ and celebrated in chapter thirteen. Here it caps and governs every other command: do everything in love. Courage and strength and firmness are all to be exercised in love, and Paul ends the letter with his own love to the church in Christ Jesus.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's unmerited favor in Christ. Paul opened the letter with grace and now closes it the same way: the grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. Everything in between, correction, teaching, and hope, is bracketed by grace, the free favor of God that both saves and sustains His people.

basic.context: Paul brings the letter to a close with practical matters. He gives instructions for a collection to help the poor Christians in Jerusalem: set money aside every week, planned and regular, so it is ready when he comes. He shares his travel plans, commends Timothy and mentions Apollos, and then fires off a series of short commands: be watchful, stand firm, be courageous, be strong, and do everything in love. He honors faithful workers, sends greetings, and ends with a longing cry for the Lord to come and a blessing of grace.
basic.hermeneutics: These closing verses show doctrine landing in ordinary church life. The teaching of the whole letter, and especially the resurrection hope, now takes the shape of generous giving, faithful labor, watchful courage, and mutual love. Paul's personal plans and greetings are not mere filler; they reveal a network of real churches and workers bound together in the gospel, and they model how truth becomes practice.
basic.originalLanguages: The collection is a logeia, a planned, regular gathering of gifts for the needy. The closing charge opens with gregoreo, be watchful, a call to spiritual wakefulness. Every command is then governed by agape, love: do everything in love. And the letter ends as it began, with charis, grace, the grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.
basic.typology: The collection for Jerusalem echoes the sharing of Israel's tribes and points to the one new people of God, Jew and Gentile, united in Christ and caring for one another. The first day of the week, the day of resurrection, becomes the rhythm of Christian giving and gathering, a weekly witness to the risen Lord.
basic.christ: Christ is the center even of these closing lines. The giving flows from His grace, the labor is the work of the Lord, the love is His love, and the great longing is for His return, Maranatha, Come O Lord. The letter ends where it must, in the grace of the Lord Jesus and love in Christ Jesus.
basic.god: God is the giver of the open door for effective work, the Lord who permits or redirects our plans, and the source of the grace that frames the whole letter. He is building one people from many nations, and He calls them to love, to give, to stand firm, and to wait eagerly for His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Second Corinthians 8 and 9 unfold the same Jerusalem collection and the theology of cheerful giving. Acts 20 records Paul's travels through Macedonia and his companions. Revelation 22 echoes the cry Come, Lord Jesus. Romans 15 explains the offering for the poor saints in Jerusalem.
basic.oneStory: The letter ends by weaving the young Corinthian church into the worldwide people of God: giving to distant believers, hosting traveling workers, greeting sister churches, and crying out together for the Lord to come. The grand truths of resurrection and gospel come down to a weekly offering, a firm stand, a loving deed, and a longing heart, all held in the grace of Christ.

context.literary:
The chapter is built from the small hinges the Corinthians themselves supplied. Paul has been answering a letter from them, and the phrase 'Now about', in the Greek a short 'peri de', has marked each new topic since 1 Corinthians 7:1, 8:1 and 12:1. It returns at 16:1 for the collection and again at 16:12 for Apollos. Chapter 16 is therefore not a loose pile of postscripts. It is the last two items on the Corinthians' own agenda, followed by the letter's farewell.

The movement runs from money to people to a charge to a signature. Verses 1 to 4 are practical and almost administrative. Verses 5 to 12 are an itinerary, with three named workers set beside Paul's own plans. Then, in verses 13 and 14, the style changes abruptly: five staccato commands, four of them in a single verse, and then a fifth that reaches back over the whole letter, 'Do everything in love.' Verses 15 to 18 return to named people, Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, and verses 19 to 24 gather greetings from Asia, from Aquila and Prisca, from 'all the brothers', and then Paul takes the pen himself.

The placement matters. Chapter 15 ended with 'your labor in the Lord is not in vain', and chapter 16 immediately shows what such labor looks like: a purse set aside on Sunday, a scholar who will come when he can, a household that served. The great argument for resurrection is not left in the air. It lands in a ledger, a travel diary and a list of names.

The closing also circles back to the letter's opening. The letter began with grace, 1 Corinthians 1:3, and ends with grace, 16:23. It began by naming Corinth's divisions over leaders, 1:12, and ends by naming leaders who serve and are to be honored, 16:15 to 18. Love, the subject of chapter 13, is the final word of the charge in 16:14 and of Paul's own farewell in 16:24.
context.historical:
The collection was one of the great projects of Paul's ministry, and this is its first appearance in his letters to Corinth. It began with an agreement. When Paul met the leaders in Jerusalem they asked only that he 'remember the poor', and he says he was eager to do it, Galatians 2:10. Years earlier the church at Antioch had sent relief to Judea during a famine, Acts 11:27 to 30. Now Paul has already given the same instructions to the churches of Galatia, 16:1. He would carry the matter through Macedonia and Achaia, and in Romans 15:25 to 27 he explains it as a debt: the Gentiles have shared in Jewish spiritual blessings and so owe a material return.

The letter was written from Ephesus, 16:8, probably in the mid fifties of the first century, and Pentecost, the harvest pilgrimage feast, gives Paul's timetable. His 'great door' at Ephesus was real and costly. Acts 19 describes both the extraordinary growth of the word there and the riot of the silversmiths, and Paul says elsewhere that he fought 'wild beasts' at Ephesus, 15:32.

The people named here sketch a map of the early church. Timothy had already been sent ahead, 4:17 and Acts 19:22. Apollos, the eloquent Alexandrian of Acts 18:24 to 28, had been the figurehead for one Corinthian party, 1:12, yet Paul calls him 'our brother' and pleads for him without a trace of rivalry. Aquila and Prisca, Jewish believers who had been expelled from Rome and had worked with Paul in Corinth, Acts 18:1 to 3, were now in Ephesus with a church meeting in their house. The churches of the time owned no buildings; they gathered in homes, and wealthier households like that of Stephanas made the work possible.

Paul's habit of taking the pen at the end, 16:21, was common among those who dictated letters through a secretary, as Romans 16:22 and Galatians 6:11 show.
context.canonical:
The collection runs through the whole Pauline corpus and gives chapter 16 a long canonical echo. It is arranged in Galatians 2:10 and 1 Corinthians 16:1 to 4, urged at length in 2 Corinthians 8 and 9, explained theologically in Romans 15:25 to 31, and finally on its way to Jerusalem in Acts 20:4, where the delegates of the churches are named, with a backward glance in Acts 24:17, where Paul tells Felix he came to bring his people gifts for the poor. Paul uses four different words for it across these passages, fellowship, service, grace and blessing, and each word is a small theology of giving.

The command to be watchful and strong is old. Joshua is told 'Be strong and courageous' on the edge of the land, Joshua 1:6 and 1:7, and the Greek Old Testament uses the same verb that Paul uses for 'be men of courage'. Jesus uses the watch language in Gethsemane, 'Watch and pray', Matthew 26:41, and in the Olivet discourse, Mark 13:35 to 37, and Paul turns the same call on a church that has been dozing in its own cleverness.

The ending of the letter is picked up elsewhere. 'Greet one another with a holy kiss' reappears in Romans 16:16, 2 Corinthians 13:12 and 1 Thessalonians 5:26, and Peter has 'a kiss of love', 1 Peter 5:14. The Aramaic Maranatha in verse 22 is answered in the last prayer of the Bible, 'Come, Lord Jesus', Revelation 22:20, and is found in the early Christian meal prayers preserved in the Didache. The anathema belongs with Paul's earlier use of the same word in Galatians 1:8 and 9 and in 1 Corinthians 12:3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul intends the Corinthians to hear three things at once. First, that the collection is a settled matter, not a fresh appeal. He gives a simple method, a portion set aside each week, so that nothing is done under pressure when he arrives. Enthusiasm that is not planned tends to fade, and a plan fixes that. He also builds in accountability: the church itself will choose the people who carry the gift, 16:3, and Paul will accompany them if that is wise, 16:4. He protects himself and them from any suspicion about the money.

Second, he wants them to see how ordinary faithfulness is bound to the gospel they have just heard defended in chapter 15. The plans, the travel and the greetings are not an afterthought. They show an apostle who does not rule the church from a distance but works inside a web of mutual obligation, asking permission, 'if the Lord permits', 16:7, honouring a younger worker, 16:10 and 11, and respecting the independence of Apollos, 16:12.

Third, the charge of verses 13 and 14 is aimed at the whole community and at its habits. A church that had prized speech and knowledge is told to stay awake, stand firm and be strong, and then to measure everything by one yardstick. Paul also calls them to give weight to people like Stephanas who have no platform and a great deal of service, 16:15 to 18. The final warning and the final prayer, 16:22 to 24, put the hearers before the Lord himself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Some of this chapter is plainly local. The collection was for the saints in Jerusalem at one moment in history, and Paul's travel plans, the timing of Pentecost and the people named belong to the narrative. Nothing here commands every church to send money to Jerusalem, or to keep Paul's schedule, or to greet with a literal kiss. The kiss was a cultural sign of family affection, and what carries forward is the affection and the unity it expressed, not the specific gesture.

What does carry forward is the principle behind the instructions. Giving should be regular, proportionate to what one has received and planned rather than improvised, 16:2. It should be handled with integrity, and it should reach real needs among fellow believers. The call to stay alert, stand firm and act in love in verses 13 and 14 is directly prescriptive, as is the instruction to give honour to those who give themselves to service. Even the practice of meeting on the first day of the week is described as the settled pattern behind the instruction rather than commanded as a new law, and the New Testament nowhere gives a detailed rubric for it. Where this passage describes, we learn; where it commands, we obey. The skill is in noticing the difference.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by setting something aside 'on the first day of every week'?

views.label: A private store kept at home
views.case: The Greek phrase beside each person can mean 'by himself' or 'at home', and the verb for saving up suggests a treasury building at home. On this reading Paul simply wanted a fund accumulated in each household so that no collection would have to be taken when he came, which is exactly what 16:2 says.

views.label: A gift brought to the Sunday gathering
views.case: Others point to the first day of the week as the day believers met, Acts 20:7, and to the word 'collections' in verse 2. They read it as a weekly offering collected as part of worship, so that the pooled sum was ready when Paul came.

debates.bearing: Either way the pattern is the same: giving is planned, regular and proportional, and Sunday is already the church's natural rhythm. The text does not require one reading to be sure of the practice.

debates.question: How should Maranatha in 16:22 be read?

views.label: 'Our Lord, come!' (marana tha)
views.case: If the Aramaic is divided as marana tha, it is an imperative prayer. This fits Revelation 22:20, 'Come, Lord Jesus', and the way the formula closes the meal prayers in the Didache, so that the church cried out for the Lord's return when it gathered at the table.

views.label: 'Our Lord has come' (maran atha)
views.case: Divided as maran atha, it is a statement that the Lord has come or is present. The word then recalls the incarnation or the Lord's presence among his people, and the curse before it becomes a warning given in his presence.

debates.bearing: The Greek 'Come, O Lord' in the Berean Standard translation follows the first reading, and the surrounding hope for his appearing in chapters 15 and 16 favors it. Both readings hold that the Lord Jesus, addressed as Lord, is the one to whom the prayer is made.

debates.question: Whose will is meant in 'it was not at all his will' about Apollos in 16:12?

views.label: Apollos's own will
views.case: The pronoun most naturally refers to Apollos, who for his own reasons, perhaps to avoid becoming the focus of rivalry, 1:12, did not want to go just then. Paul accepts his decision without complaint.

views.label: God's will
views.case: Some ancient and modern readers take 'will' to be the will of God, the same word that opens the letter, 1:1, and so read it as a sign that the timing was not yet right under God's direction.

debates.bearing: Paul's actions are the same in both readings: he urges, he respects the answer and he leaves the timing in other hands. That is a model of how leaders honor each other without commanding each other.

study.originalLanguages:
Four words and constructions in the chapter reward a slower look. The first is the word for the collection itself, logeia, in verses 1 and 2. It is a plain, business like word for a gathering of money, and Paul does not dress it up here. That is striking, because elsewhere he describes the same project with richer vocabulary. In Romans 15:26 it is koinonia, a sharing or partnership. In 2 Corinthians 8:4 and 9:1 it is diakonia, service. In 1 Corinthians 16:3 the gift is a charis, a grace, and in 2 Corinthians 9:5 it is eulogia, a blessing. Paul says the same thing four times, and each term gives a different dimension: money as fellowship, as service, as grace and as blessing.

The second is the group of verbs in verse 13. 'Be on the alert' is gregoreite, the call to stay awake, the verb of the watching servants in Mark 13:35 to 37 and of Jesus in Gethsemane. 'Stand firm' is stekete, a verb Paul likes for holding a position, as in Philippians 4:1 and 1 Thessalonians 3:8. 'Be men of courage' is andrizesthe, literally 'act like men', and the Septuagint uses the same verb for 'be courageous' in Joshua 1. 'Be strong' is krataiousthe. All four are present imperatives, which means a continuing way of life rather than a single act. They are bundled into one verse and then followed by a short sentence, in Greek simply 'all your things in love let be done', which is the only verse of the chapter that governs the rest.

The third is the pair of words for Stephanas and his household. They were the aparche of Achaia, the firstfruits, a term from the harvest offering of Leviticus 23:10 that Paul also uses for Christ in 15:20. They 'devoted themselves', literally 'appointed themselves' to the service of the saints, using the verb tasso, which means to put in an assigned place. Service here is a self appointed rank that no committee gave. In verse 16 the instruction to 'submit' uses hypotasso, the same verb as in 14:34 and 15:27, but here it is an ordering of respect for those who serve, not a chain of command.

The fourth is the unusual word anathema in verse 22, and the Aramaic maranatha that follows it. Anathema is the Septuagint's common word for something devoted to destruction, the Hebrew herem, as in Deuteronomy 7:26. Paul uses it in Galatians 1:8 and 9 against those who preach a different gospel. What makes verse 22 surprising is the verb in the condition. Paul does not write the verb of Christian self giving love, agapao, but phileo, the verb of personal affection and loyalty. The test of a believer is not agreement with a creed but affection toward the Lord. The Aramaic form, left untranslated for Greek speakers, suggests a prayer that came from the earliest Jewish believers in Jerusalem and was preserved exactly because it was precious.

typology.type: The collection and the nations bringing wealth to Zion
typology.fulfillment: The prophets expected the nations to bring their wealth to Jerusalem, Isaiah 60:5 to 7 and Isaiah 66:20. Many interpreters see Paul's collection as a quiet fulfillment: Gentile churches carrying a gift to the Jewish believers' city. The correspondence is real, but the direction and the motive are new. No tribute is demanded; the gift is a free sharing, Romans 15:27, and it goes to the poor saints, not to a temple. Paul's own explanation is that the Gentiles owe a material return for spiritual blessings. The type falls short of a literal pilgrimage because the new temple is the people of God themselves, 1 Corinthians 3:16.

Israel presented the first sheaf of the harvest to the LORD as a pledge that the whole harvest would follow, Leviticus 23:10 and 11. Paul calls Stephanas's household the firstfruits of Achaia, 16:15, and a few verses earlier Christ himself is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep', 15:20. The pattern is that the first and the small guarantee the many. Christ is the real pledge of the resurrection harvest, and each new household of faith is a smaller pledge of the nations to come. The type is imperfect because Stephanas's household offered a first conversion, not an atoning sacrifice.

typology.type: Maranatha and the coming of the LORD
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament speaks again and again of a day when the LORD comes, Psalm 96:13 and Zechariah 14:5. In verse 22 Paul takes a prayer that belongs to God and addresses it to Jesus, whom he calls simply 'Lord'. The correspondence is that Israel waited for her God to come, and the church waits for Jesus to come. The escalation is that the one who comes is the same Lord who has already come in flesh, so the waiting is built on a first appearing. The prayer is not complete until 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and Revelation 22:20 are fulfilled.

typology.type: The anathema and the devoted thing
typology.fulfillment: In the Old Testament a thing under the ban was handed over to God for destruction, and Achan's theft of it brought trouble on the camp, Joshua 7. Paul uses the same word in verse 22 for the person who refuses love for the Lord. The correspondence is that rejection of the one true Lord cannot sit inside the covenant community. In Christ the pattern deepens, because he took the curse on himself, Galatians 3:13, so that the only remaining curse falls on those who finally turn from him. The Old Testament ban was concrete and communal; the New Testament warning is addressed to individuals of conscience.

study.christ:
Christ is the unseen center of a chapter that mentions him only briefly, and it is worth noticing where he appears. He is first the reason for the collection. The saints in Jerusalem are the people among whom the gospel began, and the Gentile churches give because 'the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings', Romans 15:27. He is also the pattern for the gift. Paul will say in 2 Corinthians 8:9 that Christ, 'though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor', and the weekly portion in verse 2 is a small echo of that. A Corinthian setting aside a sum on the first day of the week is imitating, in coins, what the Lord did in person.

He is the reason for the day. The first day of the week is the day on which Jesus was raised, Luke 24:1 and John 20:19, and that is why believers gathered then, Acts 20:7. Paul's arrangement is therefore the earthly counterpart of chapter 15: those who have heard that death has been defeated put a share of their income aside on the very day that the news was first told.

He is the owner of the work. Timothy is 'doing the work of the Lord, just as I am', 16:10. In 15:58 the Corinthians were told to excel in the work of the Lord, and here is the work: guarding a young servant from contempt, sending money to the poor, welcoming Stephanas.

He is, above all, the Lord whose coming is invoked. 'Come, O Lord!' in verse 22 addresses Jesus with a title that the Greek Old Testament uses for the God of Israel. The entire letter has held that tension: one God, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, 8:6. The early Aramaic prayer simply takes it for granted that the exalted Jesus is the one to whom the church cries for his return.

He is the final word of the letter. 'The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you' in verse 23 repeats the opening of the letter, and 'My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus' in verse 24 gives a second, personal blessing. Even Paul's love is located 'in Christ Jesus'. There is no love for the Corinthians in the abstract, and none that is apart from the one who loved them first.

A word of caution is in order. The chapter does not turn the collection into an allegory of the cross, and neither the first day of the week nor the greeting of the kiss is a coded picture of Christ. The connections above rest on what Paul and the other New Testament writers say in plain words, and what the chapter does is show a church whose giving, labor and longing are all addressed to the same Lord.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is the Lord who permits and directs. Paul's plans are held with an open hand: 'if the Lord permits', 16:7. That small phrase says that the sovereign God is the one in whom a missionary's timetable rests, and it is not a mere pious formula, for Paul has just spoken of a 'great door for effective work' that has 'opened' to him, 16:9. God opens doors, and God also allows opposition to stand beside the open door. The same verse puts the two together, and a God who is able to open a way is not obliged to take every obstacle out of it.

He is the God who builds a people across geography. The collection, the greetings from Asia and from the church in Aquila and Prisca's house, the delegation from Corinth to Paul, all witness that the congregations are not separate clubs. They belong to one family in many cities. God is not the patron of an individual Christian experience but of a body, and the body's care for its poorer members is part of its nature.

He is the God of love in action. The charge 'Do everything in love', 16:14, has no exceptions, and it is directed at a church that was tempted to treat its gifts and its theology as achievements. By giving it as the last commandment before the greetings Paul affirms that God's own character is the measure for everything the community does.

He is also the God who judges. Verse 22 pronounces a curse on those who do not love the Lord. This is no outburst of temper. It is the voice of a Jewish apostle who knows that the covenant God demands whole hearted loyalty, Deuteronomy 6:5, and who has already used the word in Galatians 1:8 to protect the gospel. The same chapter that closes with a curse closes with grace, and the two belong together: grace is not cheap, and the warning is not hopeless, because it is addressed to those still within hearing.

And he is the God who waits to be met. Maranatha is both a longing and a confession that the Lord will indeed come. That means the church is not self sufficient. It lives between a past act and a future arrival, and its worship is full of that tension.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to bring the budget and the diary to the same altar as the creed. A congregation that sings of resurrection and does not set aside money for the poor has not yet heard the whole of its own song. And a congregation that gives in love and watches for its Lord is already praying the last prayer of the Bible.

crossReferences.note: The Jerusalem leaders' only request was to remember the poor, and Paul says he was eager to do it. The collection of 1 Corinthians 16 is the fulfillment of that promise, which shows that the project was not Paul's personal idea but part of a shared agreement between Jew and Gentile branches of the church.

Paul's most complete explanation of the collection, written from Corinth as he prepared to carry it. Macedonia and Achaia were 'pleased' to give, and Paul adds that they 'owe it', because the Gentiles share in Israel's spiritual wealth. It supplies the theological reason that the practical instructions in 1 Corinthians 16:1 to 4 assume.

Paul holds up the Macedonians, who gave out of deep poverty, and turns to the Corinthians to finish what they began a year earlier. He grounds the gift in the example of Christ's own generosity and in an ideal of equality, so that one church's plenty meets another's need. It develops the same principle that 1 Corinthians 16:2 sets out in outline.

Luke lists the men who accompany Paul with the collection from the churches, including Sopater, Aristarchus, Gaius and Timothy. They are the 'letters' and 'those you recommend' of 1 Corinthians 16:3 in practice: delegates chosen by the churches, so that no one could suspect Paul of handling the money alone.

The riot in Ephesus shows what Paul meant by 'many oppose me' in 1 Corinthians 16:9. The 'great door' brought such success that the silversmiths who made shrines of Artemis rioted. Opposition and opportunity arrived together in the same city and in the same season.

God commands Joshua three times to be strong and courageous, and he adds that the courage rests on the word of God and the presence of the LORD. The Greek verb for courage in this passage is the one Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 16:13, and the setting is similar: a people about to enter a great task need steadiness more than novelty.

Jesus asks his sleeping disciples to watch and pray so that they will not fall into temptation. The verb for watchfulness is the same one Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 16:13. A Corinthian church that has been tempted by wisdom, status and quarrelling is called back to the first and simplest discipline the Lord gave.

Paul greets Prisca and Aquila, who risked their necks for his life, and 'the church that meets at their house'. The same couple and the same house church appear in 1 Corinthians 16:19, now in Ephesus. Together the two passages show how mobile and hospitable this couple were, and how much of early church life depended on private homes.

The Bible ends with the Spirit and the bride saying 'Come', the Lord's answer 'Yes, I am coming soon', and a final 'Come, Lord Jesus' followed by a blessing of grace. It is the same cry as Maranatha, and the same movement from longing to grace, written at the end of the canon rather than the end of one letter.

Paul closes another letter with a prayer that God would keep his people blameless until the coming of the Lord Jesus, a greeting with a holy kiss and a blessing of grace. It shows the same sequence as 1 Corinthians 16: love among brothers, a holy greeting and a closing look toward the Lord's return.

study.oneStory:
The Bible began with a garden in which God supplied everything and humanity was to tend it, Genesis 2:15. Sin turned the garden into a place of need, and from that point the story is full of a peculiar movement: the people who have more share with those who have less, and God himself is the first to give. Joseph feeds a famine stricken world, Genesis 41 and 47. The law makes room for the poor in every harvest, Leviticus 19:9 and 10, and the prophets measure Israel by how she treats the needy, Isaiah 58:6 and 7. The collection of 1 Corinthians 16 belongs to that stream.

It also belongs to the story of how the one people of God gets made from two. Ephesians 2:14 to 16 says Christ has broken the wall between Jew and Gentile. The collection is that doctrine becoming something one can hold in the hand: Corinthian coins in Jerusalem hands, Gentile churches paying back what they received from the Jewish ones. A thread that began with Abraham, 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you', Genesis 12:3, reaches in this small gift a visible knot.

The chapter looks backward to chapter 15, where the resurrection is the hinge of history, and forward. Its call to be watchful, firm and loving describes the way of life of a people who live between the first and the second coming of Christ. Its curse and its prayer make the point that history is not simply drifting. The Lord will come, and those who love him and those who do not will be shown for what they are.

The letter's last words connect with the last words of the whole Bible. Revelation 22:20 and 21 repeats the cry, 'Come, Lord Jesus', and the blessing of grace. In the new creation the collection will have no more purpose, for no one in the new Jerusalem will be poor, Revelation 21:4. The watching will end in sight, the courage will end in rest, and the love Paul asked them to do everything in will become the air of the city itself, because God himself will dwell with his people. Until then, the weekly portion, the open door, the household that serves, and the cry of Maranatha are the way a people who have heard the resurrection news learn to live in the old world.

quiz.q: What does Paul instruct about the collection for the saints?

options.text: Each is to set aside money on the first day of every week, so the gift is ready when he comes.
options.note: Regular, planned, proportionate giving so no last-minute collections are needed.

options.text: A single large gift should be demanded from the wealthy only.
options.note: Paul asks each one to give, weekly and proportionately, not only the wealthy.

options.text: Give generously by impulse whenever moved, with no set pattern.
options.note: Generosity is right, but Paul urges deliberate, weekly setting aside, not only impulse.

options.text: The church should not give to believers elsewhere.
options.note: The whole point is a gift for the poor saints in Jerusalem.

quiz.q: What are the four commands in verse 13?

options.text: Be on the alert, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong.
options.note: A compact charge to watchfulness, steadfastness, courage, and strength.

options.text: Give, pray, fast, and tithe.
options.note: Good practices, but not the four commands of this verse.

options.text: Be silent, be still, be hidden, be safe.
options.note: The commands call for active watchfulness and courage, not withdrawal.

options.text: Stand firm, be strong, be humble, and be quiet.
options.note: Stand firm and be strong are right, but the verse calls for watchfulness and courage, not humility and quiet.

quiz.q: What governs all the commands, according to verse 14?

options.text: Love: do everything in love.
options.note: Courage and strength are all to be exercised in love.

options.text: Reverence and the fear of the Lord.
options.note: Godly reverence matters, but Paul names love as what must govern everything.

options.text: Personal ambition.
options.note: The opposite: everything is to be done in love, not ambition.

options.text: Strict rule-keeping.
options.note: Not rule-keeping but love is to shape everything.

quiz.q: What does the cry Maranatha express?

options.text: The longing prayer of the church, Come, O Lord, for Christ's return.
options.note: An early Aramaic prayer voicing the hope of the Lord's coming.

options.text: A pronouncement of judgment on those who do not love the Lord.
options.note: That is the preceding clause, let him be under a curse; Maranatha itself is the prayer, Come, O Lord.

options.text: A closing word about the collection for the saints.
options.note: The collection was earlier in the chapter; Maranatha is a prayer for the Lord's coming.

options.text: A greeting to the churches of Asia.
options.note: The greetings are separate; Maranatha is a cry for Christ to come.

quiz.q: How does Paul end the letter?

options.text: With the grace of the Lord Jesus and his love in Christ Jesus.
options.note: The letter closes in grace and love, framing everything in Christ.

options.text: With a final list of rules to obey.
options.note: He closes with grace and love, not a rulebook.

options.text: With a warning that all is hopeless.
options.note: He ends in grace, love, and the hope of Christ's coming.

options.text: With greetings and a holy kiss, but no final blessing.
options.note: He does send greetings, but the letter closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus and his love in Christ.

questions: Paul asks each believer to set aside a gift regularly on the first day of the week. What would planned, cheerful, proportionate giving look like in your own life?
An open door for effective work stood before Paul even though many opposed him. Where might God be opening a door for you in the face of opposition?
Verse 13 calls you to be watchful, firm, courageous, and strong. Which of these do you most need to grow in right now, and how?
Everything is to be done in love. Where are you tempted to be right, or strong, or firm without love, and how would love reshape it?
The church cried Maranatha, Come O Lord. How alive is your longing for Christ's return, and how might it change the way you live this week?

translationNotes.note: The first day of every week is Sunday, the day of Christ's resurrection, which was becoming the Christian day of gathering; the instruction ties regular giving to that weekly rhythm.
Prisca is the same person called Priscilla in Acts; Paul uses the more formal form of her name alongside her husband Aquila.
Maranatha is an Aramaic expression preserved from the earliest church, rendered here Come, O Lord; it voices the church's prayer for Christ's return and is echoed in Revelation 22:20.
